latin.677: §. XII. Tandem Nobilissimus Autor quatuor paragraphis, Testimonia Lutheranorum quatuor, in tantum lacessat, in quantum ex iis adstruxeram: Oralem Manducationem, Fidei Fundamentum neutiquam attingere.
latin.678: (1.) CALIXTI Senioris, cujus Viri Autoritatem dumtaxat imminuere satagit, apud omnes interim bonos moderatosque, antiquitatis item Ecclesiasticæ studiosos, perduraturam, etiamsi non infallibilis, nec à nobis, istô potissimum nomine, habenda sit, quòd Pontificios non minus, salvô licet Tridentino Concilio, Protestantica multa anathematizante, quàm Reformatos, salva horum Synodo Dordracenâ, dogmata quædam Lutherana obliquè quidem & per latus Arminianorum improbante, nullo verò anathemate feriente, in unius Ecclesiæ Christianæ Societatem advocat. Testimonio intereà hujus Viri contra Fundamentalitatem Oralis Manducationis inconcusso persistenti superaddendum & illud est, quô idem dissidium de ea Protestanticum, Unioni Protestantium Ecclesiasticæ nihil quicquam officere posse, inde probat, quòd Spiritualiter Corpus Christi manducantes Reformati, non minus Oraliter id manducent, quàm ipsi Lutherani, cùm Oralis Manducationis veritas, non à Manducantium Opinione, sed à Voluntate Institutionis Cœnæ, dependeat. Jud. de Controver. n. 76.
latin.679: (2.) PUFENDORFII, quòd hic Illustris Autor, Systemati suo articulorum Fundamentalium, etiam Articulum de Orali Manducatione, inseruerit: Quasi verò Pufendorfius merorum Fundamentalium Systema complexus sit, nullis admixtis Præterfundamentalibus; vel non mitius, de Reformatorum sibi visis in S. Cœna erroribus, senserit, quàm Disputator noster vellet. Legatur ipse §. 2. & sigillatim §. 63. de Cœna, & facilè apparebit, Manducationem corporis Christi Oralem, quà talem, inter fidei Christianæ fundamenta haudquaquam numerasse eum: Ita enim finit dictum suum: Ceterum si utraque pars Protestantiæ bonâ fide profiteatur, in S. Cœna Corpus & Sanguinem Christi re verá ac propriè edi ac bibi, deque partis ab ipso beneficiis participari, CONTROVERSIA REMANET CIRCA MODUM COMESTIONIS ET BIBITIONIS, IPSIUSQUE PRÆSENTIÆ CORPORIS ET SANGUINIS CHRISTI; quem utique captum humanæ rationis transcendere agnoscunt, eoque ratiociniis res geritur, ubi rationi locus non est. pag. 229.
latin.680: (3.) HULSEMANNI, quem de solis Auditoribus & Laicis inter Reformatos, non autem de Doctoribus & Clero, verba fecisse, vel contra omnem sensum, enuntiat Aut.: Nam de Reformatorum doctrina judicium ferre, nec tamen Doctores eorum subinuere, uti alogon, ita ab accuratione & acumine Hülsemanniano alienissimum existit.
latin.681: (4.) LUTHERI, cujus Testimonium miratur à me allegatum, quippe, ex Epistola, Reformatis infesta, depromptum, maximè, cùm notum prætereà sit, Lutherum Marpurgi, ubi de Cœna S. inter Lutherum & Zwinglium disceptatum potissimum fuerat, errores Zwinglianos, interque eos, Oralis Manducationis inficiationem, adeò exitiales & fundamentum christianæ fidei impetentes æstimasse, ut proptereà tandem ita inter Disputantes conventum sit: Pacem se habituros mutuis scriptis, si fortè Deus Zwinglianis Cor aperiat.
latin.682: Resp. (1.) Testimonium Lutheri tantò præstantius esse & efficacius, quantò magis ab irascente Zwinglianis Luthero profectum est. (2.) Lutheri iram non adeò versam fuisse in Oralis Manducationis Negationem Zwinglianam, quàm in hypothesin, per iram, Zwinglianis imputatam, ab his verò fotam nunquam, quasi in S. Cœna nil nisi panis & vinum habeatur, id quod sexcenties Bucerus Luthero demonstravit in Scriptis suis Anglicis. (3.) Marpurgi non ita conventum esse, ut Autor refert ex Epistola Lutheri ad Præpositum, sed ut Chytræus refert in Hist. August. Confessionis, cujus verba plus semel citata ita habent: Etsi verò an verum corpus & Sanguis Christi CORPORALITER in pane & vino Cœnæ Domini præsens sit, hoc tempore non concordavimus: Tamen UNA PARS ALTERI Christianam dilectionem declarabit, & UTRAQUE PARS Deum omnipotentem diligenter orabit, ut NOS Spiritu suo in vera sententia confirmet, Amen.
latin.683: Ceterum ut numero Probationum quinario Autoris, quô pro Fundamentalitate Oralis Manducationis, depugnavit, Numerum Testimoniorum Lutheranorum contra eandem, quin totum Sacramentum Cœnæ, quatenus Fundamentalibus fidei dogmatibus annumeratur, adæquemus, agedum adhuc unum, in medium olim allatis quatuor, nunc superaddemus, & quidem cujusdam Professoris, non ita pridem Wittebergensis, cujus Auctoritas apud Autorem major fuerit, quàm Calixti: Est verò Testimonium ANDREÆ SENNERTI in Exercitat. ejus Theologica de Articulis fidei fundamentalibus §. LXIV. his verbis legendum: Sacramenta succedunt, & quidem illa in genere vel communi primùm considerata. Quæ, quòd neque ad ARTICULOS FIDEI FUNDAMENTALES, NEQUE PRINCIPALES, retulimus, nemo mirabitur facilè (utut in re majoris momenti nemini vicissim præjudicamus) si consideret nobiscum, (1) quod Apostolus Rom. IV, 11. eadem signacula, sigilla fidei nominet; adeoque hoc ipso à Substantia vel Substantialibus fidei notanter distinguat. Et certè (2) per naturam suam fidem non tam (extra initiationis sacr.) ingenerant aut producunt: quàm (3) qua sigillorum in contractibus, fœdere, testamentis, natura aut ratio vel conditio est, Symbola tanquam quædam certa, externa & visibilia, fidem confirmant adaugentque. Unde (4) cùm in Vet. & Novo Testamento, Substantialia eadem & una sint … sigilla gratiæ tamen sunt fueréque diversa … adeoque (5) Necessaria, quidem sunt ratione Instituentis, & vi mandati divini: (6) SED NON SIMPLICITER VEL ABSOLUTE AD FIDEM VEL SALUTEM, quod & dictis & exemplis Scripturæ S. poterat probari.
latin.684: Et paucis intersertis pergit Sennertus: (8) Necessaria porrò adeo, sunt ad salutem secundum quid, ut suprà dictum, ratione mandati divini, quatenus ex abundanti DEUS fidem nostram munire signis & sigillis certis voluit … quibus (9) in casu necessitatis carere quidem possumus extrà jacturam fidei & salutis æternæ. Tandem, quò dicta de Sacramentis in genere, etiam Sacramento cœnæ applicentur, §. LXV. ita concludit: Quod de Sacramentis in genere vel communi dictum, idem esto judicium de singulis in specie & V. & N. Testamenti, Circumcisione, Agno Paschali, Baptismo & S. CŒNA.

pass_a.677: §. XII. At length the most noble Author in four paragraphs so lashes the four Lutheran Testimonies, insofar as from them I had built: that Oral Eating in no way touches the Foundation of Faith.
pass_a.678: (1.) Of CALIXTUS Senior, whose man’s authority he is content merely to diminish, though among all good and moderate men, and students of ecclesiastical antiquity, it will endure — even if not infallible, nor to be held by us chiefly on that name, because he summons into one Christian Church society Pontificians no less (Trent safe though anathematizing many Protestant things) than the Reformed (Dort safe though obliquely disapproving certain Lutheran dogmas through the Arminians’ side, yet striking with no anathema). Meanwhile to this man’s unshaken testimony against Oral Eating’s Fundamentality is to be added also that by which he proves the Protestant dissension about it can in no way hinder Protestant ecclesiastical Union — because the Reformed who eat Christ’s Body spiritually eat it no less orally than the Lutherans themselves, since Oral Eating’s truth depends not on the eaters’ Opinion but on the Will of the Supper’s Institution. Jud. de Controver. n. 76.
pass_a.679: (2.) Of PUFENDORF, that this illustrious Author inserted into his System of Fundamental articles even the Article of Oral Eating: As if Pufendorf had embraced a System of mere Fundamentals with no Prefundamentals mixed in; or had not felt more mildly about Reformed errors he saw in the Holy Supper than our Disputant would wish. Let him be read at §. 2. and especially §. 63. on the Supper, and it will easily appear he by no means numbered Oral Eating of Christ’s body as such among the foundations of Christian faith: For thus he ends his saying: But if both parts of Protestancy in good faith profess that in the Holy Supper Christ’s Body and Blood are truly and properly eaten and drunk, and that the benefits from him are participated, THE CONTROVERSY REMAINS ABOUT THE MODE OF EATING AND DRINKING, AND OF THE PRESENCE ITSELF OF CHRIST’S BODY AND BLOOD — which they acknowledge transcends human reason’s grasp, and so the matter is handled by reasonings where reason has no place. p. 229.
pass_a.680: (3.) Of HULSEMANN, whom the Author declares — even against all sense — to have spoken only of Auditors and Laity among the Reformed, not of Doctors and Clergy: For to pass judgment on the Reformed’ doctrine and yet not glance at their Doctors is as irrational as it is most alien to Hülsemannian accuracy and acumen.
pass_a.681: (4.) Of LUTHER, whose Testimony he marvels I alleged, namely drawn from an Epistle hostile to the Reformed — especially since it is moreover known that Luther at Marburg, where the Holy Supper was chiefly disputed between Luther and Zwingli, so judged Zwinglian errors, and among them the denial of Oral Eating, deadly and assaulting the foundation of Christian faith, that at last the disputants agreed: they would keep peace by mutual writings if perhaps God should open the Zwinglians’ Heart.
pass_a.682: Reply (1.) Luther’s Testimony is so much the more excellent and efficacious as it proceeded more from Luther angry at the Zwinglians. (2.) Luther’s anger was not so turned against the Zwinglian Negation of Oral Eating as against a hypothesis anger imputed to them, never cherished by them — as if in the Holy Supper nothing but bread and wine were had — which Bucer six hundred times showed Luther in his English Writings. (3.) At Marburg it was not so agreed as the Author reports from Luther’s Epistle to the Provost, but as Chytraeus reports in the History of the Augustan Confession, whose words cited more than once run: Although whether Christ’s true body and Blood be CORPORALLY present in the bread and wine of the Lord’s Supper we have not this time agreed: Yet ONE PART will declare Christian love to THE OTHER, and BOTH PARTS will diligently pray almighty God that HE confirm US by his Spirit in the true opinion, Amen.
pass_a.683: But that we may match the Author’s fivefold number of Proofs for Oral Eating’s Fundamentality with the number of Lutheran Testimonies against the same — indeed against the whole Sacrament of the Supper as numbered among faith’s Fundamental dogmas — come, let us now superadd one more to the four formerly brought forward, and indeed of a Professor not long since of Wittenberg, whose Authority with the Author will have been greater than Calixtus’s: It is the Testimony of ANDREAS SENNERT in his Theological Exercise on the fundamental articles of faith §. LXIV, to be read in these words: The Sacraments follow, and indeed those first considered in genus or common. That we have referred them neither to FUNDAMENTAL ARTICLES OF FAITH NOR PRINCIPAL ones, no one will easily marvel … if he consider with us (1) that the Apostle Rom. 4:11 names them seals, seals of faith, and so notably distinguishes them from the Substance or Substantial things of faith. And certainly (2) by their nature they do not so much generate or produce faith (outside the initiation sacrament) as (3) after the nature of seals in contracts, covenant, testaments, they confirm and increase faith as certain external visible Symbols. Whence (4) … (5) they are Necessary by reason of the Institutor and force of divine mandate: (6) BUT NOT SIMPLY OR ABSOLUTELY FOR FAITH OR SALVATION, which could be proved by Holy Scripture’s sayings and examples.
pass_a.684: And with a few things inserted Sennertus continues: (8) Further they are necessary to salvation in a qualified sense, as said above, by reason of divine mandate, insofar as God from abundance willed to fortify our faith with certain signs and seals … which (9) in a case of necessity we can indeed lack without loss of faith and eternal salvation. At last, that what was said of Sacraments in general may also apply to the sacrament of the Supper, §. LXV. he thus concludes: What was said of Sacraments in genus or common, let the same judgment be of each in species of both O. and N. Testament — Circumcision, the Paschal Lamb, Baptism, and the HOLY SUPPER.

677: §.XII: the Author spends four paragraphs attacking the four Lutheran testimonies Strimesius used.
Those testimonies had shown Oral Eating does not touch the foundation of faith.
678: (1) Calixtus Senior: the Author only tries to shrink his authority; among moderate antiquity-minded readers it still stands — even if not infallible, and not mainly because he beckons Papists and Reformed into one church society without Dort anathemas on Lutheran dogmas.

Add also Calixtus’s point (Jud. Controv. n.76): Protestant split over Oral does not block union — Reformed who eat spiritually also eat orally if Oral truth hangs on the institution’s will, not the eaters’ opinion.
679: (2) Pufendorf: inserting Oral into a fundamentals system does not prove he packed only fundamentals, or that he judged Reformed Supper “errors” as harshly as our Disputant wants.

Read §.2 and especially §.63: he does not number Oral eating as such among faith’s foundations. If both sides confess true eating and drinking of body and blood, the fight left is about the MODE of eating/drinking and of presence (p.229).
680: (3) Hulsemann: the Author claims — against all sense — he spoke only of Reformed auditors and laity, not doctors and clergy.
To judge Reformed doctrine while ignoring their doctors is irrational and alien to Hülsemann’s accuracy.
681: (4) Luther: the Author marvels Strimesius cited a letter hostile to the Reformed.

He adds Marburg: Luther ranked Zwinglian errors — including denying Oral eating — as deadly assaults on faith’s foundation, so the sides agreed to keep peace in writing until God opened Zwinglian hearts.
682: Replies: (1) testimony from an angry Luther is stronger, not weaker; (2) the anger aimed less at denying Oral than at the false charge that the Supper is only bread and wine — which Bucer proved false to Luther many times in the English writings.

(3) Marburg’s terms are Chytraeus’s, not the Author’s Provost-letter version: they had not agreed whether body and blood are corporally present, yet each side would show Christian love and both would pray for the Spirit’s confirmation. Amen.
683: To match the Author’s five proofs, Strimesius adds a fifth Lutheran witness — Wittenberg’s Andreas Sennert (§.LXIV), whose weight with the Author tops Calixtus.

Sennert: sacraments (as a class) are neither fundamental nor principal faith articles — Paul calls them seals of faith (Rom 4:11), distinct from faith’s substance; they confirm faith like contract seals; necessary by mandate, but not simply or absolutely for faith or salvation.
684: Sennert continues: they are necessary to salvation only in a qualified sense (God’s abundant seals); in necessity we may lack them without losing faith or eternal salvation.
§.LXV: what holds of sacraments in general holds of each — circumcision, Passover lamb, baptism, and the Holy Supper. Stop §.XII before Annotatio VI (Indignorum).

677.gloss: in no way touch the Foundation of Faith

679.gloss: THE CONTROVERSY REMAINS ABOUT THE MODE
